label: Person
name: Adrian II
summary:
Pope Adrian II (reigned 867–872) faced one of the most complex pontificates of the ninth century, caught between the Carolingian succession crisis, the Photian Schism that was rending the Eastern Church, and the evangelical expansion into the Slavic world. Elected at approximately 80 years old after twice refusing the papacy, Adrian II brought advanced age and limited energy to an office that demanded extraordinary political skill.

The Photian Schism — the bitter controversy over whether Photius or Ignatius was the legitimate Patriarch of Constantinople — dominated Adrian II's pontificate. The Fourth Council of Constantinople (869–870), which condemned Photius and restored Ignatius, was convened under his authority and is recognised as an Ecumenical Council in Catholic tradition. This settlement, however, proved temporary — Photius was later restored.

Adrian II's pontificate also coincided with the mission of Saints Cyril and Methodius to the Slavs. The two Greek brothers, who had created the Glagolitic alphabet to translate Scripture into Old Church Slavonic, visited Rome in 867 to seek papal support for their Slavic mission. Adrian II gave them his blessing and approval, authorising the use of Slavonic in the liturgy — a decision of enormous cultural consequence for the subsequent development of Slavic Christianity and literacy.
